Sanquhar Declaration
sang'kêr dek-lê-rā'shūn
n. (the declaration posted at Sanquhar, Dumfriesshire, 22 June 1680, by Richard Cameron and twenty armed Covenanters, disowning Charles II)
Sanquhar, from Gaelic sean càthair, old fort; declaration, from Latin declarare, to make clear.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Sanquhar Declaration was read aloud at the market cross of a small Dumfriesshire burgh by a band of twenty men who then nailed it to the cross and rode away. It disowned Charles Stuart as king, on the ground that he had broken the covenants he swore at his coronation, had usurped the crown rights of Christ over His church, and had made war on his own subjects for worshipping God. It declared war against him as a tyrant and against James, Duke of York, as a papist successor. One month later Cameron was killed at Airds Moss. Nothing in British history quite matches the arithmetic: twenty men against a kingdom, in writing, signed. Act 5:29 is its first premise. Act 4:12 is its second, that the sole headship of Christ is not transferable, and that no earthly supremacy may stand in that place. Mat 10:28 explains how twenty men do such a thing and then go home to supper.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a declaration as an affirmation; a public announcement or proclamation; and a tyrant, as a despotic ruler; a cruel master; an oppressor.

expand to see more

DECLARA'TION, n. An affirmation; a public announcement or proclamation of a fact or an intention.

TY'RANT, n. A monarch or other ruler or master, who uses power to oppress his subjects; a cruel master; an oppressor.

SUPREM'ACY, n. State of being supreme or in the highest station of power; highest authority or power.

Key Scripture

Act 5:29 — "Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men."

Act 4:12 — "Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved."

Mat 10:28 — "And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell."

Psa 11:3 — "If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?"

Modern Corruption

Twenty men published a declaration of war against a king because he had claimed a headship that belongs to Christ.

expand to see more

The theological nerve of Sanquhar is the crown rights of Christ over His church. The Stuart supremacy was not merely oppressive; it asserted that the king determines the government, worship and discipline of the church of God. Act 4:12 says there is no other name under heaven given among men whereby we must be saved, and the exclusivity there is total. A magistrate who makes himself the church's head has stepped into the one place that is occupied.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What presses now is softer and harder to see: the state claiming to define what a church may teach, whom it may employ, and which doctrines count as acceptable. The principle to recover is that the church's obedience to the magistrate is real but bounded, and that the boundary is not a matter of preference. Mat 10:28 supplies the courage; Act 5:29 supplies the rule.
